newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa says no magic formula for Zairean peace.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa says no magic formula for Zairean peace.

text.p: South Africa is pressing ahead with its efforts to bring peace to Zaire, but has no magic formula to succeed where others have failed, Deputy Foreign Minister Aziz Pahad said on Tuesday.

South Africa was in constant touch with U.N. and Organisation of African Unity (OAU) special envoy Mohammed Shanoun and its next course of action would be based on his advice, Pahad said in an interview.

"We feel that we should not have too many initiatives going and if the special envoy is now visiting the region we should wait for his report and in consultation with him decide what other role South Africa can play," Pahad said.

He added that international humanitarian and aid agencies were increasingly concerned that Zaire, where Tutsi-led rebels are seeking to overthrow veteran President Mobutu Sese Seko, was on the verge of collapse into outright civil war.

Zairean rebel radio said on Tuesday that its forces had advanced to within 10 km (six miles) of the third city, Kisangani, and predicted the government stronghold would fall to them within days. There was no independent confirmation that the rebels were so close to the city.
Pahad said plans were going ahead for heads of state including South African President Nelson Mandela to meet Mobutu in Nairobi or Kinshasa on March 19 to explore options for peace.
He said he expected a decision this week on whether the meeting would involve only Kenya, South Africa, Zimbabwe and Cameroon, or whether other regional states would be included.

Pahad and South African Deputy President Thabo Mbeki acted as go-betweens in Cape Town recently between Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila and a Mobutu envoy. The two opposing sides did not meet directly.
The week-long initiative failed to bring the two sides to a truce in their conflict in eastern Zaire, but Pahad said it had not failed.

"It was important to get the essence of what both sides wanted, feed it into the process and see if we couldn't fast-track the process and get them together. I think we have contributed, accelerated the process.
"We are very keen that we continue facilitating the process so that dialogue between the two sides, direct dialogue, can start," he said.
But Pahad said Africa often expected too much of South Africa's two-and-a-half-year-old democracy and of Mandela.
"The quicker we get some of these diplomats to understand that all the problems of Africa cannot be solved with some South African magic wand, the better.
"There is a feeling that South Africa has no other interest but to try to resolve conflicts. There is this Mandela syndrome, that we know how to avoid conflict.

"While we cannot ignore some of the conflicts that are emerging in Africa, we must be realistic about our capacity.... South Africa could run the risk of getting ivolved in too many conflict issues without the necessary preparation," he said.
Pahad said the priority in the search for a Zairean solution remained to consolidate the three or four separate initiatives into one backed by the U.N., the OAU and the European Community.

"Zaire borders on nine countries. If that country explodes or implodes...South Africa would suffer the consequences if that explosion takes place - mass migration, arms proliferation, destabilisation generally. It will affect us."
